Thursday and Thursday night: A cold front will continue to track 
across eastern WA into ID into Thursday morning, before weak high
pressure builds in Thursday night. A line of light precipitation 
will track over central into eastern WA through mid-morning, 
progressing to ID from late morning to afternoon. Some lingering 
orographic showers are also possible around the Cascades, but 
these look isolated. Precipitation chances wane for tonight

Snow levels will be around 4.5-5.5kft, locally near 3.5-4kt near 
the Canadian border in the morning. So mainly valley rain and 
mountain snow is forecast, though some rain/snow mix is possible 
near Canadian border valleys early. Rain amounts are generally 
forecast to be less than 0.10 inches; the lowest are forecast in 
the lee of the Cascades to central WA at a trace to 0.02 inches. 
An exception will be the Cascade crest, where storm total 
precipitation amounts from Wednesday night through this afternoon 
are forecast between 0.10 to 0.30 inches. Most of the that will 
have fallen overnight/early this morning. Mountain snow 
accumulations will generally be less than 0.5 inches, except 
locally up 1 inch near the Cascade crest. The main passes that may
see accumulation will be Washington and Sherman, but they will be
on that lighter range. 

The other impact will be the low clouds and fog. Fog will be most
likely this morning and again later tonight into Friday morning. 
Low clouds were slow to erode yesterday and that slow erosion is 
forecast to today over the eastern third of WA and north ID 
Valleys; with some models suggesting the stratus does not break 
significantly until mid to late afternoon, possibly not until 
sunset. Winds do increase slightly over southeast WA, with gusts 
of 10-15 mph before dissipating in the late afternoon. The winds 
should limited the fog somewhat in the afternoon and evening. 
However late tonight into Friday morning the decreasing winds and 
recent rain, along with the southeast flow developing seems a 
moderate pattern for fog development. I do not think the NBM is 
handling it well and the RRFS is very expansive with it, while the
REFS is more tempered. Somewhere in the middle of all this 
supports the development across the Upper Columbia Basin, Palouse,
Spokane/CdA area and northeast valleys. Confidence in intensity 
and coverage is only fair, so those details will be fine-tuned; 
but we seem to be having some foggy days of late.

Highs will be in the mid-40s to mid-50s today, with some upper 
50s in the deeper basin. Lows tonight will be in the largely in 
the 30s, with some upper 20s in the sheltered northern valleys.

Friday to Saturday: The Inland NW transitions to stronger zonal 
flow, with a warm front lifting into the area. Friday looks mostly
cloudy, with the combination of the stratus/AM fog and middle to 
high clouds spreading over the region. Precipitation chances come 
to the Cascades Friday morning, expanding toward the Upper 
Columbia Basin in the afternoon and across northeast WA and north 
ID Friday night as the warm front lifts north. Snow levels start 
near 3.5-4.5kft Friday AM, rising to 6-9kft by Friday evening. So 
this will be mainly mountain snow and valley rain, changing to 
mostly rain. By Saturday the moisture lifts north, leading to 
drier weather with more sun. Highs will be in the mid-40s to lower
50s Friday, warming to the 50s to low 60s Saturday. Friday will 
be a bit breezy over the Okanogan Valley to Upper Columbia Basin, 
with gust near 10-20 mph. Some of that breeziness will be possible
around the Palouse Saturday.

Saturday night to Wednesday: The pattern remains progressive with
a series of systems tracking by the area; agreement starts to 
break down by Wednesday. The strongest of these systems comes by 
Saturday night into Sunday, with sharp trough and 115kt jet. 
Precipitation chances expand into the Cascades Saturday night and 
spread toward the eastern third of WA and ID by Sunday. The 
westerly flow will tend to shadow out lee of the Cascades and 
limit the QPF over the eastern CWA. Snow levels start at 6-8kft, 
dropping to 4.5-7kft by Sunday evening with lowest near the 
Cascades. Drier weather comes Sunday night into Monday, then 
additional waves will bring precipitation chances across the area 
Monday night, Tuesday and Wednesday. Snow level drop to between 
3-6kft Monday, lowest again near the Cascades, the moderate toward
5.5-7.5kft Tuesday into Wednesday. 

These latter system will have a bit better chance of measurable 
precipitation away from the Cascades, but overall wetting rain 
chances will be limited, except in the Cascades. For the Cascades 
for the Saturday night/Sunday system 0.25 to 0.75 inches are 
forecast, then 0.15 to 0.60 inches with each of the next couple 
systems. As for snow amounts, right now it is early but it is 
translating to 1 to 4 inches of snow, locally higher around the 
higher mountains Sunday, with the main potential impact for the
